An MIQCP-based multi-objective optimal operation strategy for
renewables-integrated smart distribution systems considering transformer
loss of life and environmental emissions
Amir Bagheri
a
, Saleh Mobayen
b , *
, Nasrin Osali
c

Department of Electrical Engineering, University of Zanjan, Zanjan, Iran

ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Smart distribution system
Optimal operation
Renewable energies
Transformer LOL
Multi-objective optimization
MIQCP model
ABSTRACT
Owing to growing electricity demand and environmental concerns, renewable-energy-based distributed gener-
ations (DGs) are widely integrated into today ’ s distribution systems. However, high penetration of renewables
DGs (RDGs) requires additional investments in high-cost step-up transformers connecting RDGs to the grid. On
the other side, regarding variability of RDGs ’ output power, the connecting transformer ’ s capacity is not
completely utilized in a considerable time period. In this paper, a smart-grid technology-based scheduling model
is proposed to efficiently utilize the free capacity of existing transformers without investing on new ones. The
model is based on dynamic thermal rating (DTR) and loss of life (LOL) feature of transformer. The developed
approach is formulated as a mixed-integer quadratic constrained programming (MIQCP) as a convex model to
obtain global optimum solutions. The conducted model is treated as a multi-objective optimization with LOL
minimization as well as emission reduction. The proposed multi-objective model is implemented using
ε -constraint method where the final solution is selected by fuzzy-satisfying and max - min techniques. The model
is implemented in GAMS and the optimization is accomplished by GUROBI solver to show efficacy of the pro-
posed approach. The simulations demonstrate the capability of conducted approach in managing the CO2
emission as well as transformer loss of life. Among different Pareto solutions, the best solution reduces the CO2
emission by 11.7% while the transformer ’ s aging is decreased by 19.2% demonstrating environmental, eco-
nomic, and technical advantages of the proposed model.
1. Introduction
1.1. Background and motivation
Distribution networks have the task of receiving electricity from
transmission systems at high voltage (HV) levels and delivering it to
consumers at medium or low voltage (MV-LV) levels [ 1 – 3 ]. Due to radial
topology of distribution systems, the network operators are usually
engaged with high voltage drop and power losses. These problems are
more highlighted when the load demands of consumers are grown [ 4 ].
To resolve the mentioned problems, different short-term and long-term
solutions are employed by distribution network operators and planners,
such as distribution network reconfiguration (DNR) [ 5 , 6 ], optimal
capacitor banks placement [ 7 , 8 ], and reinforcement/installation of lines
(feeders) [ 9 , 10 ]. Another alternative is the use of DG units which are
widely integrated in today ’ s electric power grids [ 11 ]. DG units bring
several advantages for distribution systems, such as reducing power
losses and voltage drop, reliability enhancement, releasing capacity of
equipment, and postponing the need for installation/reinforcement of
lines and HV/MV transformers [ 12 ]. Among the DG units, the
renewable-energy-based ones, like wind and photovoltaic (PV) units are
under more attention due to their cleanliness and
environmental-friendly features. They also relieve the concerns of
countries regarding depletion of fossil-based fuels [ 13 ]. However,
addition of more PV and wind capacities is subject to some limitations.
An important limitation is the capacity of LV/MV step-up transformers
connecting the wind and PV farms to the MV electric grid. Traditionally,
expanding the capacity of PV and wind farms must be implemented in
line with replacement of existing transformers with the ones having

output powers of wind and PV units are time-dependent regarding the
variation of wind speed and solar radiation, their connecting trans-
former rarely reaches to its nameplate rating, and will have extra ca-

more transformer capacity with expansion of wind and PV farms ca-
pacity may not be economical. Instead, in today ’ s power systems,
introduction of smart-grid technologies (SGTs) has enabled network
operators to have a real-time supervision and control on different
equipment such as lines, switches, transformers, generating units, etc.
[ 16 – 20 ]. One of SGTs is dynamic transformer rating (DTR). The thermal
rating of a transformer (in MVA) is dependent on its constructional
characteristics (such as windings, iron core, cooling system, etc.) as well
as weather parameters such as ambient temperature [ 21 ]. As the
weather parameters are varied in different time, the rating will be also a
variable quantity. However, the transformer designers report the ther-
mal capacity on the “ Nameplate ” based on the worst-case weather
condition (i.e. maximum ambient temperature). This rating is called as
static transformer rating (STR) which is a conservative value that will
occur only in short time periods [ 22 ]. If the transformer is equipped with
SGTs, its real-time capacity, known as DTR, can be calculated in an Y

manner to be used in real-time scheduling of distribution system [ 23 ].
On the other side, if the transformers are not replaced by high-capacity
ones when PV and wind farms are expanded, the loading of transformer
will be increased even above its STR. Overloading of transformer brings
about its temperature rise, insulation degradation, and possible loss of
life [ 24 ]. Overloading and LOL of transformer are against expansion of
renewable energy units and emission reduction. Therefore, it is an
essential issue to smartly manage the transformer loading and temper-
ature regarding penetration increase of renewable energy units. The
current paper will address this issue and developed a model to simul-
taneously manage these two challenges. Subsequently, the related pa-
pers around this subject are reviewed to highlight the gap of existing
researches and contributions of the present work.
1.2. Literature review
There have been different researches around dynamic thermal rating
of transformer and its utilization in optimal operation of transmission
and distribution systems. Ref. [ 25 ] presents a risk-based strategy for
managing of distribution transformers based on their dynamic rating.
The load and ambient temperature are provided as probabilistic inputs
obtained from quantile regression forests. The insulation thermal ageing
because of transformer overloading in terms of rewinding cost is
compared with the cost of installing new transformer. This paper does
not consider distribution system constraints and power flow equations,
instead different scenarios of load profile are considered for the
transformer.
To expand capacity of wind farms, Ref. [ 26 ] investigates the possi-
bility of using DTR capability of step-up transformers without making an
investment on new transformers. The transformer loss of life is con-
verted to a cost to compare it with installation cost of new transformers.
A single-node system along with a 6-node one followed by DC power
flow equations are used to investigate the conducted approach. It is
worth mentioning that the DC model of power flow does not reflect the
network behavior appropriately as it disregards voltage and reactive
power limitations.
Demand response (DR) and DTR are used in [ 27 ] to increase reserve
of transformer. The reserve estimation based on a linear programming
optimizes the DR volume and operation over a given time interval. The
thermal limit, maximum power, and the aging effects of transformer are
considered in the mathematical model. This paper ignores the electric
grid topology and network-related constraints; i.e. the investigations are
on a single-bus system.
Authors in [ 22 ] proposed a day-ahead scheduling model for power
system integrated with large wind power plants. The model exploits DTR
as well as dynamic line rating (DLR) in order to minimize operation, load
shedding, and wind power curtailment costs. The DC model of optimal
power flow (DC-OPF) is utilized to consider system constraints. The
results show positive effect of simultaneous usage of DLR and DTR. The
work of [ 22 ] is extended in [ 28 ] to use AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF)
for network calculations as well as to incorporate uncertainty of problem
input parameters. Ref. [ 29 ] is the extended version of [ 22 ] which con-
siders network-constrained units commitment instead of OPF consid-
ering AC power flow equations. The energy storage system (ESS) as well
as phase shifting transformer (PST) are considered in [ 30 ] to develop the
models of [ 22 , 28 – 30 ] and to exploit more capacity of wind farms and
reduce the operational costs. However, none of the references [ 22 ,
28 – 30 ] have considered the transformer loss of life and insulation
thermal aging.
Ref. [ 14 ] combines the thermal model of transmission lines and
transformers to determine the potential increase in wind farm capacity.
The impact of higher thermal limit on the LOL of the transformer is
compared to the amount of curtailed wind and the potential revenue
from the added wind farm. The network constraints are not considered
in this paper.
Short-term and long-term planning of wind farm is implemented in
[ 15 ] by the aid of DTR. Optimal wind farm capacity is determined by a
mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model. As the top-oil relation
of transformer is nonlinear based on the IEEE Clause 7, its linearized
model is employed to keep the model linear. The simulations obtain the
relation between net present value of investment and the capacity of
wind farm transformer. A sensitivity evaluation is accomplished to
assess the consequences of wind speed, price of electricity, and lifelong
of the transformer for the wind farm ’ s feasibility. This paper does not
consider LOL issues, and it disregards network-related constraints.
In [ 31 ], an optimal operation strategy is proposed for distribution
networks incorporating DTR of transformer. Also, management of
network flexibility options including on-load tap changer (OLTC),
switchable capacitor banks, and static VAr compensator (SVCs) are
coordinately implemented in order to minimize the total operation cost
and to maximize the dispatched power of PV units connected to LV sides
of the transformers. The model is a convex one with a single objective
function composed of several cost items summed up with the weighting
factors. The most recent research is [ 32 ], where dynamic line rating and
dynamic transformer rating are co-optimized to obtain the most eco-
nomic operational plan subject to lines ’ conductor as well as trans-
former ’ s hot-spot temperature limitations. This work is in transmission
network level where the optimization model is a single-objective
non-linear programming (NLP).

1.3. Research gap and paper ’ s contribution
Based on the literature, Table 1 compares in summary the features of
the literature with the present work. In this paper, a convex MIQCP-
based multi-objective network-constrained optimal operation strategy
is proposed to simultaneously maximize scheduling of wind and PV units
and minimize transformer loss of life. At first, the fundamental equations
of dynamic transformer rating and its insulation aging are described and
incorporated in AC-OPF model of distribution network. Then, the
problem is formulated as a multi-objective optimization considering all
the network, transformer, and renewable energies limitations. After-
wards, the non-linear terms are linearized to form a convex optimization
model obtaining global optimum solution within GAMS environment. In
brief, the contributions of this paper can be outlined as follows:
• Integration of DTR relations into optimal operation of smart distri-
bution systems;
• Simultaneously considering transformer loss of life and environ-
mental emissions using a multi-objective optimization;
• Linearizing non-linear relations to obtain a convex MIQCP optimi-
zation model;
• Considering all the distribution network constraints in the proposed
operation model;
• Maximizing scheduling of wind and PV units as renewable energy
sources along with life management of transformers.

2.4. Proposed scheduling model
The proposed problem is a multi-objective scheduling optimization
of smart distributions system integrated with PV and wind farms by
considering DTR and LOL of transformers connecting the farms to the
network.

environmental emission as shown in (14). It includes emission of CO2
corresponding to the power received by distribution system from the
upward grid. The upward grid is the transmission system within which
the centralized thermal generators are located. The thermal generating
units produce greenhouse gases for the aim of electricity generation, and
cause CO2 emission. P

2.4.2. Problem constraints
• Power flow relations

optimization model to be non-convex. In this regard, the line flow based
(LFB) model of load flow, as convex formulation, has been used in this
paper according to (16)-(23) [ 9 ]. The parameters used in the relations
have been defined in the nomenclature. In the LFB power flow, instead

2.4.4. Multi-objective optimization
The proposed model in this paper is a multi-objective optimization
including minimization of environmental emission and minimization of
loss of life of the transformers. These two objectives are contradictory.
There are two approaches for handling of multi-objective optimization.
One is to convert it to a single-objective one using weighting factors [ 22 ,
28 , 30 ], and the other is to provide Pareto-optimal solutions [ 36 , 37 ]. For
the latter case, normal boundary intersection (NBI) and ε -constraint
techniques are two well-known methods to prepare Pareto-optimal so-
lutions [ 38 ]. These techniques are generally similar to each other in
transforming the multi-objective problems to a series of single optimi-
zation problems. Their difference is in distribution of Pareto-optimal
solutions within the search space. In this paper, ε -constraint method is
employed to obtain Pareto-optimal solutions within GAMS environ-
ment. In this method, one of the objective functions is selected to be
optimized while the other(s) are converted into additional constraints,
leading to a solution that can be proven to always be Pareto-optimal
[ 38 ]. For the aim of multi-objective optimization in this paper, an iter-
ative process is implemented as the following steps to minimize the two

2.4.5. Optimization tool
GAMS is a powerful software package for optimizing various prob-
lems with variety of variables and constraints. Having suitable solvers,
this software is able to find the solutions of linear and non-linear opti-
mization models with real and binary variables [ 33 ]. The basic model of
the proposed problem was non-linear and non-convex, which is hard to
solve, and its solution does not guarantee the global optimum point. By
the aid of the proposed convexifications, the model has been converted
to a mixed-integer quadratic constrained programming (MIQCP), which
is convex model. In this paper, the “ GUROBI ” solver in the GAMS is
employed to find the global optimum solution for the proposed model
[ 39 ].
3. Numerical study
3.1. Describing the test network
The analyses of this paper are performed on the IEEE 33-bus system
depicted in Fig. 2 . The system is a 12.66kV network at the MV level and
400V at the low-voltage level. The peak load demand of network is
3.715MW and 2.3MVAr. The complete data related to the branches and
loads of this network is given in [ 40 ]. There are two renewable energy
sources in this network at low-voltage (LV) level, which is 400V. A PV
farm with the characteristics of Table 2 is connected to bus 30. Also, a
wind farm with the rated power of 1MW is attached to bus 14. The rated,
cut-in, and cut-out speeds of the wind farm are 14m/s, 4m/s, and 25m/s,
respectively. The wind and PV farms are connected to the medium
voltage (MV) side through two 400V/12.66kV DTR-equipped step-up
transformers, named as Transformers 1 and 2. Table 3 shows the pa-
rameters for the thermal model of the two transformers. As the original
network is exposed to high voltage drop, two 600kVAr capacitor banks
are installed at buses 14 and 30 to compensate for the reactive power.
The hourly profile of the wind speed, solar radiation, ambient temper-
ature, and load demand are given in Fig. 3 .

5. Conclusion
This paper proposed a smart-grid technology-based optimal opera-
tion strategy to coordinately manage renewable energy sources along
with transformers loss of life. The developed model is formulated as a
multi-objective optimization to provide Pareto-optimal solutions using
ε -constraint method. For selection of the final solution, fuzzy-
satisfaction and max-min techniques are employed to make a promise
between CO2 emission reduction and reduction of transformers’ insu-
lation aging. The basic model was non-liner and non-convex, but using
the convexifications and linearizations, the optimization problem was
transformed to a convex MIQCP model whose solution in GAMS pro-
vides global optimum solutions. Applying the developed model on the
IEEE 33-bus network demonstrated that by smart scheduling, distribu-
tion system operator can appropriately schedule the wind and PV farms
without decreasing the insulation life of the transformer. It was
demonstrated that almost the same scheduling of PV and wind farms
(the same CO2 emission) is fulfilled with about 19.2% of insulation
aging, while the CO2 emission is decreased by 11.7%. In this way, a
clean as well as economical operation is fulfilled for the distribution
system. The uncertainty of environmental parameters including wind
speed, solar radiation, and ambient temperature may affect the results
obtained in this paper. These uncertainties can be modeled by different
probability distribution functions (PDFs) such as Weibull, Beta, and
